member.summary: Ranks completion candidates for a partially typed console line.

remarks.para: Separate from , which stays exactly as it was. That method answers a narrow question — "what common prefix can Tab safely insert?" — and its prefix-only, first-token-only behaviour is the correct answer to it. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Diagnostics.LogRouter
member.summary: The logger a process runs on: filters each record by and hands it to every sink.

remarks.para: One router per process, built first, before anything that logs. Sinks can be added at any point after: the in-game console exists only once the graphics device does, and the startup that came before it is exactly what somebody opening the console wants to read. So the router keeps the most recent records in a replay buffer and plays them to a sink when it is added.

Safe from any thread. Records are handed to sinks one at a time under a lock, which keeps their order identical in every sink and makes adding a sink atomic with the replay; the sinks themselves only format or queue, so the lock is held for microseconds. A disabled call never takes it.
A record flushes every sink before the call returns, since it is normally the last thing a process says.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.IrradianceVolume
member.summary: A grid of probes holding how much light arrives at each point in the level, and from where.

remarks.para: Why a grid of probes at all. The screen-space bounce in the stage before this can only use surfaces the camera can see, so a wall just off screen neither shades nor colours anything, and anything indoors is lit by whatever happens to be in frame. A probe volume knows about the geometry the camera cannot: each probe was asked, once, what it can see in every direction, so a soldier standing in a doorway is lit by the room he is in rather than by the view.

Why the visibility is baked and the light is not. The expensive question is geometric — what can this point see — and in this game the answer never changes: the levels are static, and the sun is a fixed direction per mission rather than a moving body. So the transfer is traced once at load and only the colours are applied per frame, which makes relighting a multiply rather than a trace. That is the classic precomputed-transfer bargain, and it is a particularly good one here because the thing it gives up — light that moves — is a thing this game does not have.

What it stores. First-order spherical harmonics: one constant plus three directional terms per colour channel. That is four numbers to describe light arriving from every direction at once, and evaluating it for a surface is a dot product. Second order would resolve sharper gradients, at twice the storage and with ringing artefacts that need windowing; L1 is what an irradiance field wants, because irradiance is already a cosine-blurred version of the light around it and has almost no high-frequency content left to resolve.
Distances are in metres and positions are absolute world coordinates, matching everything else the renderer is handed.

remarks.para: The counterpart to MipChainBuilder, which is the right filter for a picture and the wrong one here. That builder decodes each channel from the display encoding, averages, and re-encodes — correct for a photograph of a wall, and a systematic bias on a map that carries a normal's x and y, a roughness and a material flag. Decoding a normal's x as though it were a brightness and re-encoding the mean pushes the average towards the larger of its inputs, so two opposing slopes no longer cancel and the surface leans a little further with every level.
It also drops the alpha weighting, which exists so a cut-out's transparent gaps cannot darken the wire's colour. A detail map's alpha is a material channel and every texel of it counts.

Why a chain at all. A surface drawn smaller than its map samples a scattering of unrelated texels, and for a normal map each of those is a different lighting direction — which reads as sparkle, not as detail. Without a chain the sampler also falls back to nearest mip selection and loses anisotropy entirely, because both are choices between levels and there is only one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.MaterialMapGenerator
member.summary: Derives the surface maps a physically-based renderer needs from a diffuse texture that has none.

remarks.para: I.G.I. ships one texture per surface and nothing else — no normal map, no roughness, no statement anywhere about what a surface is made of. That was not a limitation of the art; it is what a renderer of that generation could consume. A physically-based model has four inputs and the data answers one, so the other three have to be derived.

This is invented data, and the code should say so. It is a deliberate divergence and nothing under vanilla reads a byte of it. What it buys is the difference between brick that reads as brick when the sun crosses it and brick that reads as a photograph of brick pinned to a flat card — which is a larger visible gap than any amount of indirect lighting.

The pipeline, and why it is not just a Sobel filter. Treating luminance as height directly is the obvious approach and it is wrong in a specific, very visible way: it is right wherever a texture is dark because it is recessed, and wrong wherever a texture is dark because somebody painted it that way. A black stripe painted on flat concrete becomes a trench. So the luminance is frequency-separated first — the broad, smooth part of an image is overwhelmingly its colour, and the fine part is overwhelmingly its relief. Height is taken from the fine part alone, and everything else is derived from that height rather than from the picture:

item.description: Luminance, high-passed against a wide blur, becomes the height field.
Scharr gradients over two octaves of that height become the normal.
A horizon search over the height field becomes ambient occlusion.
Local high-frequency energy, plus curvature, becomes roughness.

remarks.para: Metallic is not attempted and cannot be. Nothing in a diffuse texture distinguishes painted steel from grey paint — the difference is in how each behaves under light, which is exactly the information the texture does not carry. Guessing it would put a mirror finish on half the level. That channel comes from authored data or it stays at zero.

Everything wraps. These textures tile — the ground, every wall, every crate — so the pixel left of column zero is genuinely the last column. Clamping instead flattens all four edges, which shows up as a seam grid over the whole level and is the single failure that makes derived maps look homemade.
Pure: no device, no GL, no file system. Pixels in, pixels out, so the part hardest to be confident about can be tested directly.

member.summary: Roughness, from the local standard deviation of the height field.

remarks.para: A surface whose neighbourhood varies has structure finer than the geometry can show, and structure finer than the geometry can show is exactly what roughness means physically. So the measure is the spread of the height field about its own local mean — the same quantity every other generator of these maps uses, over a window rather than over the four adjacent texels.

The window is what makes it meaningful. Measuring against the four immediate neighbours, as the first version of this did, does not measure a surface's character at all: at that radius the only thing that varies is single-texel photographic grain, so every texture in the game came back at almost the same value and the map was flat. A neighbourhood wide enough to contain a brick and its mortar is what distinguishes brick from painted steel.

Computed from two separable box blurs rather than by sampling the window per texel — the standard deviation is the square root of the mean of the squares less the square of the mean, and both means are box filters. That makes the cost independent of the radius, which matters because a per-texel window over the whole game's art is minutes and this is seconds.

Never returns below one: a texture being smooth is not evidence that the SURFACE is polished, only that nobody painted detail on it, and polishing every blank wall in the game is the wrong reading. What is authored in materials.json stays the floor.

member.summary: Writes 8-bit RGBA PNGs.

remarks.para: The project writes BMPs where it needs an image out of the renderer, because a BMP is a header and then the pixels and needs no encoder at all. That stops being enough the moment an image is meant to leave the project — a texture export is thousands of files, and thousands of uncompressed BMPs is tens of gigabytes for data that compresses to a fraction of it.
Deliberately minimal in every direction but one: one colour type, one bit depth, no interlacing.

The exception is FILTERING, which started as filter zero on every row and is now chosen per row. That was not worth doing while the output was a few thousand small textures to look at; it became worth doing when a 4x pack of the same art turned into gigabytes. Measured over 60 of the game's textures enlarged four times, filter zero gives 19.6 MB against 35.4 MB unpacked, and choosing per row gives 11.2 MB — the filters are worth more than the deflate they feed.

The heuristic is the one the PNG specification suggests: try all five and keep whichever leaves the smallest sum of absolute signed differences. It is not optimal and does not need to be; it is one pass over five candidate rows and it recovers most of what an exhaustive search would.

member.summary: Scalar helpers whose behaviour is part of the engine's determinism contract.

remarks.para: The original game is an MSVC 6 / x87 binary. Its float-to-integer conversions go through the CRT helper _ftol, which truncates toward zero and — for NaN or out-of-range inputs — yields the x87 "integer indefinite" value (the most negative integer of the target width). .NET, by contrast, saturates such conversions since .NET Core 3.0. The conversion helpers here reproduce the original behaviour, so game logic must use them rather than a plain cast.
The main loop of the original asserts the FPU rounding mode every frame by checking that (long)(-1.75) == -1; preserves exactly that.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.IgiRandom
member.summary: The engine's own pseudo-random generator — a three-word lagged shift-and-add.

remarks.para: Transcribed from 0x4B4740 and its two wrappers. Everything that has to look random in the original draws from one of these, and the streams are picked by 0x416D20, which in the retail build ignores its argument and returns the single global stream at dword_57BABC + 44.

The generator is reproduced rather than substituted because the order and the count of the draws is part of the game's behaviour: a spread sample takes four draws in a fixed order, and the recoil's rejection loop takes an unbounded even number. A different generator would still look random and would not reproduce a shot.
The value is quantised to 1/65536: only the low sixteen bits of the accumulator are used, so yields one of 65536 values in [0, 1) and never reaches one.

member.summary: Composes the engine's three Euler angles into a rotation, as 0x4B38E0 does.
member.param: The third angle, about Z — the one a level's Gamma carries.

remarks.para: Read out of 0x4B38E0 rather than guessed. It writes Z(gamma) first (0x4B3BE0), then right-multiplies by Y(beta) (0x4B3BA0) and then by X(alpha) (0x4B3B60) — each step's arithmetic is M · R, dotting the running matrix's rows with the new rotation's columns. The three builders are the textbook axis rotations, row-major, with the drift counter of the 40-byte orientation block at their +36.
This is the one convention the engine uses for both level placements and the first-person eye (0x464BD0 builds the eye as Z(yaw) · Y(0) · X(pitch)).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f
member.summary: A 4×4 single-precision matrix, used for the view and projection transforms of the 3D pipeline.

remarks.para: The original has no 4×4 matrix type: it keeps orientation in a (Real32x9), the camera position in a (Real64x3), and applies the projection as scalar arithmetic — sx = x/z · xScale + cx — while transforming each vertex (sub_512C30). This type packs that same arithmetic into one matrix so a GPU can do it, which is a representation change, not a behaviour change.

Conventions. Elements are named MrowColumn and stored row-major. Vectors are columns, so a transform is M · v and composition reads right-to-left: projection * view * world. writes the transpose, which is the layout OpenGL uniforms want.

The layout is load-bearing. reads the sixteen elements as four four-wide vectors straight out of the struct, which is only correct while they sit in memory in declaration order with nothing between them. The attribute states that rather than relying on it, and Matrix4fLayoutTests checks it at run time so a change here fails loudly instead of producing a plausible but wrong transform.

member.summary: Composes two transforms.

remarks.para: A row of the product is a weighted sum of the whole of : row i is left[i][0]·right[0] + left[i][1]·right[1] + …, each term a scalar times a row. Written that way the sixty-four multiplies and forty-eight adds the scalar form spelled out become sixteen operations on four-wide vectors — the same arithmetic in the same order, four lanes at a time.

Not bit-identical to the scalar form on hardware with FMA: a fused multiply-add keeps full precision through the multiply where the separate operations round twice, so a product element can differ in its last bit. That is a strictly more accurate answer, and nothing in the port compares matrices for exact equality across a composition.

member.summary: One x87 register value under the control word the original runs its physics with, 0x0E7F: 53-bit precision, rounding toward zero.

remarks.para: With precision control at 53 bits every fadd, fsub, fmul, fdiv and fsqrt rounds its result to an IEEE double's significand, so a register value is exactly a double -- but rounded toward zero, where .NET rounds to nearest. Each operator here computes the round-to-nearest result, recovers the exact error with an error-free transformation (TwoSum for a sum, a fused multiply-add for a product, quotient or root) and steps one ulp toward zero when rounding went away from it.

A store through fstp dword truncates as well: . Truncating to double and then to float equals truncating once to float, so the two roundings never compound. Loads (fld dword, fld qword, fild) are exact and are the implicit conversions.

Only the order of operations the disassembly shows is reproduced: C# evaluates a * b + c * d + e as ((a * b) + (c * d)) + e, which is how the original's rigid-body code groups every sum. Never let two plain s meet in an operator -- that is .NET float arithmetic, rounded to nearest; one side must already be an .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.X87Single
member.summary: One x87 register value under the control word I.G.I. 2's client runs with, 0x0C7F: 24-bit precision, rounding toward zero.

remarks.para: Why 24 bits. The client creates its Direct3D 8 device without D3DCREATE_FPU_PRESERVE (Direct3D_CreateDevice, igi2ed 0x55BB80, behaviour flags 0x80 then 0x20), and Direct3D then sets the FPU to single precision. The game afterwards only ORs the rounding-control bits in (Real_SetFPUStateIEEE, igi2 0x444C40, called once the mode is set by Direct3D_SetMode, igi2ed 0x55BAC9, and again after every device reset and movie), so it runs at single precision, truncating. The first game kept 53 bits ().

Precision control rounds the result of fadd, fsub, fmul, fdiv and fsqrt to a 24-bit significand while the register keeps its wide exponent. Loads are exact: a double loaded with fld qword keeps all 53 bits until the next operation rounds its result. Each operator here takes 's truncated 53-bit result and truncates it again to 24 bits; truncations nest, so that equals truncating the exact result once.
As with , only the disassembly's order of operations is reproduced, and two plain s must never meet in an operator: one side must already be an .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Core.Threading.IWorkScheduler
member.summary: Where work the caller does not want to do on its own thread runs, as the platform allows.

remarks.para: A desktop has cores to spare and runs such work beside the frame loop. A browser running .NET has one thread, and a task started there does not run beside anything: it runs when the loop next yields, which a loop that is itself the page's frame callback never does in time. So the platform decides, and the callers say only what they want done.

Two kinds of work go through here, and is what tells them apart. Work whose result is needed -- the audio device, the shared animations, a level's backdrop -- is run either way, inline where nothing runs beside the caller. Work that is only an OPPORTUNITY -- decoding textures ahead of the frame that asks for them, warming the file cache -- is worth doing only where it overlaps with something, and a caller skips it where it would not.

So the work is an iterator whose every element is the end of a slice: runs slices until its budget has gone, runs all of them. Where the work divides into independent pieces, runs them all at once in parallel on a scheduler that can, and one per slice on one that cannot, so the desktop loses none of the parallelism it had.

The iterator hands its answer to the callback it is given. Cancellation -- an from inside -- finishes the job with the default answer, as the bakes have always treated it; any other exception propagates from the call that met it.

remarks.para: Supported means "this build can load and render it", not "it is finished". The sequel's levels load, its world, ground, sky, forest and water draw, and the shell can switch to it while the game is running; it has no player, weapons or AI yet, so a level opens in the free camera. Listing it as unavailable once the port could draw it would have been the shell telling the player something untrue about their own installation.
Support is still a claim about the port rather than about the disk. Whether it can actually be played from here is , which needs this AND the signature file to be present.

The data root is the installation's pc directory, not the directory above it: a retail install puts igi2.exe in pc alongside config.qvm, missions, common, language and menusystem.
